The thermal conductivity of RAM is 0.5 W/m·K, while that of aluminum is 205 W/m·K.
The specific heat of RAM is 1,200 J/kg·K, compared to 900 J/kg·K for aluminum.
The simulation showed that RAM reached a maximum temperature of 40.19°C, while metal stabilized at 34.05°C.
The surface temperature standard deviation for RAM was 3.47°C, significantly higher than the 0.88°C for metal.
RAM took 3.5 seconds to reach a stable temperature, while metal stabilized in just 1.5 seconds.
The infrared simulation showed a wider pixel brightness histogram for RAM, indicating higher infrared contrast and detectability.

The paper proposes three main design strategies to integrate infrared and radar stealth: local thermal control, layered structures with high thermal conductivity materials, and optimized thermal inertia distribution.
Varying the thickness or density of RAM across the structure can help control the thermal inertia distribution and improve the infrared stealth characteristics.
The integrated design approach aims to develop multifunctional stealth platforms that can effectively counter both infrared and radar-based detection threats.
The conflicting thermal requirements between infrared and radar stealth technologies pose a significant challenge for their integration on a single platform.
RAM generally has a lower thermal conductivity and higher specific heat compared to metal, leading to the formation of hot spots and uneven surface temperatures.
Uniform temperature distribution and low infrared contrast are critical for effective infrared stealth, while radar stealth relies on the radar-absorbing properties of materials like RAM.
Active thermal control systems that can dynamically adjust surface temperatures can help mitigate the issues caused by the thermal properties of RAM.
The simulation results highlight the importance of considering the thermal response characteristics of materials when designing integrated infrared and radar stealth systems.
The proposed design strategies aim to balance the conflicting requirements of infrared and radar stealth without compromising the individual stealth capabilities.
